scribe_response.text: Can you tell me about the home you grew up in? I was born in nineteen fifty-two in Thrissur, in Kerala, in a house my grandfather had built. It had a tiled uh roof of red clay, and in the monsoon the rain poured off the eaves in silver ropes. In the middle of the house was an open courtyard with a tulsi plant on a small stone platform. My mother watered it every morning uh before she lit the lamp, and I never saw her miss a day. My father was a schoolmaster, so the house was always full of exercise books, books waiting to be marked. He sat on the long wooden verandah in the evenings with a red pencil behind his ear. I have two sisters, Radha who was older and Meena who was younger, and um we shared one big room. We slept on woven mats, and the floor was cool red oxide that my mother polished every week. The kitchen was at the back, with a clay hearth and a row of brass vessels that gleamed like small suns. My grandmother ground rice batter on a heavy stone. I can still hear the sound of it. Even as a boy I wanted to know how things worked. So I studied the house like a machine. What happened next? I noticed that the courtyard let hot air rise and pulled cool air through, air through all the rooms. The roof beams were jackwood, and my father said they would outlast all of us. There was a well behind the kitchen. I loved to lower the bucket and count the seconds until the splash. Beside the well grew a mango tree that my grandfather had planted the year he finished the house. Our neighbour on the left was a carpenter named Kunjan, and I spent hours watching him work. He cut his joints without a single nail, and he let me hold the chisel when nobody was looking. On the right lived a widow who kept hens, and her cockerel woke the whole lane before dawn. The lane itself was red mud, which turned into a slippery river whenever the rains came. We uh walked to school barefoot with our books wrapped in banana leaf against the wet. In the evenings my father read aloud to us from old almanacs and sometimes from the Ramayana. My sisters and I sat on the verandah steps, and the oil lamp threw our shadows against the pillars. When electricity finally reached uh our lane, I was about eight years old. I remember the first bulb, a yellow thing hanging on a um twisted wire in the courtyard. Can you tell me more about that? The whole street came to look at it, and my father switched it on with great ceremony. I asked him where the light um came from. He said from a power station far away. That answer did not satisfy me at all, and I think it started the engineer in me. I badly wanted to see the wire that carried it and follow it all the way back. Food in that house was simple, rice and fish curry cooked with kokum and a little coconut oil. My mother cooked the fish in a clay pot, and she said clay held the flavour better than metal. On festival days the courtyard was drawn over with rice flour, flour patterns. Relatives arrived from distant villages and slept wherever there was a space on the floor. The house seemed to expand for them, and nobody was ever turned away. When I think of that place now, I feel the cool floor under my feet first. After that I smell wet earth and woodsmoke, and then I hear my mother calling us in for rice. It was a modest house, but it taught me that a good building breathes. I carried that idea with me for the rest of my life.
